analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking exemption from federal drinking-water law and requires disclosure of fracking chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 38 House Democrats, was referred to committee in March 2021 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would close the loophole that exempts hydraulic fracturing (fracking) from the Safe Drinking Water Act, giving the EPA authority to regulate fracking injections that can threaten groundwater. It would also require drilling companies to publicly disclose the chemicals they pump underground before and after each fracking job, and to hand over trade-secret chemical formulas to doctors and nurses in a medical emergency. The bill died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink from wells or public water supplies near them. The bill would give the EPA power to protect those water sources, and would give residents, health officials, and emergency physicians access to the list of chemicals used underground — including trade-secret formulas when someone is poisoned or injured. Communities near drilling sites currently often cannot learn what chemicals were injected near their water.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act provision that exempts fracking from underground-injection regulation, letting the EPA protect groundwater sources from fracking pollution risks [S2][S3].

Requires operators to disclose, before and within 30 days after each fracking job, every chemical used — including chemical identities, safety data sheets, and volumes — and makes that list public on an internet website [S3].

In a medical emergency, forces operators to immediately disclose proprietary or trade-secret chemical formulas to the state, EPA, or the treating physician or nurse, even without paperwork or a confidentiality agreement in place [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas drilling companies, which would bear the cost of reporting every chemical they inject, complying with EPA groundwater rules, and giving up some trade-secret protection during emergencies. Fracking operators argue these requirements raise costs and slow drilling.

drawbacks.text: New disclosure and permitting requirements would add compliance costs and paperwork for fracking operators, which the industry argues could slow domestic oil and gas production [S2][S3].

The bill lets states and EPA post chemical identities publicly while barring disclosure of proprietary formulas, but operators lose quick control over trade-secret information in emergencies — a real cost the industry has long contested [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — knowing what chemicals are being injected next to drinking water, and getting that information to a doctor during an emergency — directly answers a documented gap: fracking has been exempt from the Safe Drinking Water Act since 2005, so no federal drinking-water law covers it. The costs fall on drillers in the form of reporting and compliance. The bill would not ban fracking; it would regulate it like other underground injection is regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment subcommittee in late March 2021, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on March 26, 2021, with 33 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on March 26, 2021, and to its Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change on March 29, 2021 [S5].
No further action was taken — the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drilling companies are better off: fracking remains exempt from federal drinking-water regulation, and chemical use underground stays undisclosed to the public and to physicians outside emergencies.

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 33 original cosponsors

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in his committee for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal regulation of fracking under the Safe Drinking Water Act and chemical disclosure mandates

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would end the industry's exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act, subjecting fracking injections to EPA groundwater rules for the first time, and would require public disclosure of injected chemicals. Operators' interest in avoiding these rules runs against residents who want to know what is being pumped next to their water wells.

The bill requires disclosure of chemical identities and volumes but bars public disclosure of proprietary formulas; however, in a medical emergency operators must hand trade-secret formulas to a treating physician or state regulator immediately. Most of the time the formulas stay private, but the emergency carve-out cuts into trade-secret protection.
